title: Pester: tests that catch real bugs
summary: Describe, It, Should, BeforeAll and TestDrive in Pester 6; mocks with -ModuleName and Should -Invoke; and tests good enough to fail when the code is wrong.

steps.title: A Pester test file
body: **Pester** is PowerShell's test framework; it ships inside Windows (an ancient 3.4) and is installed in every serious
repo from the Gallery. The current release is **Pester 6.2** (September 2026). Version 6 kept v5's structure, so
almost every v5 test file you meet at work runs unchanged:
```powershell
# tests/Get-OldLog.Tests.ps1    (the .Tests.ps1 suffix is how Invoke-Pester finds test files)
BeforeAll {
Import-Module "$PSScriptRoot/../LogTools.psd1" -Force     # load the code under test
Describe 'Get-OldLog' {
BeforeEach {
$old = New-Item 'TestDrive:/old.log' -ItemType File -Force
$old.LastWriteTime = (Get-Date).AddDays(-40)
New-Item 'TestDrive:/new.log' -ItemType File -Force | Out-Null
It 'returns only files older than 30 days' {
(Get-OldLog -Path TestDrive:/).Name | Should -Be 'old.log'
- **`TestDrive:`** is a temporary folder per test file, deleted afterwards: perfect for file tests.
- Put setup code in **`BeforeAll`/`BeforeEach`**, never loose in the file: Pester first *discovers* the tests and
runs loose code then, not when the tests run.
- Common assertions: `Should -Be`, `-BeExactly` (case-sensitive), `-HaveCount 3`, `-Contain`, `-BeNullOrEmpty`,
`-Throw '*not found*'`, `-BeOfType [datetime]`. Pester 6 adds a typed style too (`Should-Be`, `Should-BeString`,
`Should-BeCollection`, `Should-Throw`); both work and you will see both.
- Run: `Invoke-Pester ./tests -Output Detailed`; in CI, `Invoke-Pester -CI` (exit code and a test-results file).

steps.prompt: This test file fails with `The term 'Get-OldLog' is not recognized`, although the module path is right. Why?
options: Loose code runs during discovery only; the `Import-Module` belongs in a `BeforeAll { }` block
steps.explain: Since Pester 5, a file is run twice: once to discover the `Describe`/`It` blocks, and again to run them. Only `BeforeAll`, `BeforeEach`, `It` and friends run in the second pass, so setup outside them is lost.

hints: In `BeforeEach`, create three files in `TestDrive:/` and set their `LastWriteTime` to 2, 40 and 100 days ago.
Test the default (`(Get-OldLog -Path TestDrive:/).Name | Sort-Object | Should -Be @('mid.log', 'old.log')`), a non-default `-Days 60`, and a case where nothing is old.
Write the file with a here-string and `Set-Content`, or `nano ~/src/LogTools/tests/Get-OldLog.Tests.ps1`.
solution: foreach ($f in @{ Name = 'new.log'; Days = 2 }, @{ Name = 'mid.log'; Days = 40 }, @{ Name = 'old.log'; Days = 100 }) {
It 'returns files older than 30 days by default' {
It 'returns nothing when every file is recent enough' {
explain: A test suite is only as good as the bugs it would catch. The checks used *mutation testing*: break the code on
purpose and see whether a test notices. A test that only runs `Get-OldLog` without checking *which* files came back
passes on every mutant: it is coverage without protection.

steps.title: Mocks: replace what you do not want to run
body: A **mock** replaces a command for the duration of a test, so you can test *your* logic without deleting files,
calling an API or rebooting a server, and then assert how it was called:
```powershell
It 'removes only the old file' {
Mock Remove-Item -ModuleName LogTools
Get-ChildItem TestDrive:/ | Remove-OldLog
Should -Invoke Remove-Item -ModuleName LogTools -Times 1 -Exactly -ParameterFilter { $LiteralPath -like '*old.log' }
**`-ModuleName` is the part everyone forgets.** Your function runs *inside* the module, and a mock defined in the
test's scope is invisible there: the **real** `Remove-Item` runs and `Should -Invoke` reports 0 calls. With
`-ModuleName LogTools` the mock is injected into the module's scope.
- `Mock Invoke-RestMethod { @{ status = 'ok' } }` returns fake data.
- `-ParameterFilter { $Uri -like '*/health' }` mocks (or counts) only matching calls.
- `Should -Invoke X -Times 0 -Exactly` proves something did **not** happen, such as nothing deleted under `-WhatIf`.
- To mock a command that does not exist on the test machine (a Windows-only cmdlet on a Linux build agent), define an
empty function with that name first, then mock it.

steps.prompt: A test does `Mock Remove-Item` (no `-ModuleName`), calls `Remove-OldLog` from the LogTools module, and `Should -Invoke Remove-Item -Times 1` fails with *was called 0 times*. What else happened?
options: The real `Remove-Item` ran inside the module and deleted the file
Pester refused to run the test
The mock ran but was not counted
steps.explain: The mock existed only in the test script's scope. The module's code resolved `Remove-Item` to the real cmdlet. On `TestDrive:` that is harmless; with a mocked REST call it might not be. Pester 6 prints the recorded calls (here `<none>`) to make this obvious.

steps.title: Prove -WhatIf never deletes
prompt: Write `~/src/LogTools/tests/Remove-OldLog.Tests.ps1`. Mock `Remove-Item` so nothing is really deleted, and assert
with `Should -Invoke`. At least **2 tests**; they must pass on the real module and fail on a copy that **deletes
even under `-WhatIf`**, and on a copy that **deletes every file, old or not**.

checks.name: at least 2 tests, all passing
checks.fail: Not yet (see what the check found).

checks.name: catches a broken -WhatIf
checks.fail: Add a test that pipes files into `Remove-OldLog -WhatIf` and asserts `Remove-Item` was called 0 times.

checks.name: catches deleting new files
checks.fail: Add a test with one old and one new file that asserts `Remove-Item` was called exactly once.

hints: `BeforeEach { Mock Remove-Item -ModuleName LogTools; ... create an old and a new file in TestDrive:/ ... }`
Test 1: `Get-ChildItem TestDrive:/ | Remove-OldLog`, then `Should -Invoke Remove-Item -ModuleName LogTools -Times 1 -Exactly`.
Test 2: the same with `-WhatIf`, then `Should -Invoke Remove-Item -ModuleName LogTools -Times 0 -Exactly`.
explain: "-WhatIf never deletes" is exactly the kind of promise that breaks silently in a refactor, and exactly the one
that matters most. A one-line `Should -Invoke ... -Times 0` keeps it true forever. In CI, `Invoke-Pester -CI` exits
non-zero on any failure and writes `testResults.xml` for the pipeline's test tab.
